Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images Prevent strategy Extreme rightwing referrals to Prevent rise 20% amid record anti-terror reporting Scheme aiming to stop people turning to terrorism has 39% overall rise in referrals in year to September 2025 Rajeev Syal Thu 6 Aug 2026 07.53 EDT Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 08.49 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A record number of people have been referred to the government’s anti-terror programme in England and Wales, with a 39% rise over the last year, including a 20% rise in referrals for extreme rightwing ideology, according to official data released on Thursday. A total of 10,293 referrals – up from 7,408 – were made to the Prevent programme in the year to September 2025, which is the highest number since records began 11 years ago. Those referrals to the scheme, which aims to stop people turning to terrorism, involved 9,957 people suspected of extremist or violent tendencies. The rise comes after officials noted a sustained and significant increase in referrals since the Southport attack in July 2024. Axel Rudakubana, who killed three girls at a dance class and tried to murder eight others, as well as two adults, was referred to Prevent three times but his case was closed over a lack of clear ideology. The figures show 2,103 Prevent referrals were because of concerns over extreme rightwing ideology – 20% of the total – up from 1,480 in the previous 12 months. There were 860 referrals (8%) about Islamist extremism, down from 945 over the previous year. Where age was known, 11- to 15-year-olds made up the largest proportion of Prevent referrals (3,655 or 36%), followed by 16- to 17-year-olds (1,379 or 13%), the Home Office said. A total of 818 referrals (8%) related to fascination with extreme violence or mass casualty attacks, 95 (1%) were for “incel” extremism – meaning “involuntary celibate”, the term given to a strand of misogynist ideology – and 32 (0.3%) for leftwing extremism, while 353 (3%) were for multiple ideologies with no dominant ideology identified. More than half (56%) of referrals were for individuals with no identified ideology. The Home Office has also published data showing the ethnicity of referrals to the Prevent programme, although the data is incomplete because it is not mandatory on the referral form. Of 5,315 referrals, 3,600 (68%) were white, 949 (18%) were Asian, 401 (8%) were black and 365 (7%) were listed as “other”. After initial screening and assessment, Prevent referrals who are deemed at risk of radicalisation may be passed to a multi-agency “channel panel”. Chaired by local authorities, these panels determine the extent of a person’s susceptibility to radicalisation, and whether a tailored package of support is necessary to address the risk. Of the 1,100 referrals taken on as a channel case in the year to September 2025 where ethnicity was known, 835 (76%) were white, 159 (14%) were Asian, 59 (5%) were black and 47 (4%) were “other”. Nearly one in five of those referred to the programme – 18% – were autistic, while 36% had at least one mental health or neurodiversity condition listed on their Prevent record. Jacob Smith, the team leader on freedom of expression and belief at Rights & Security International (RSI), said this was a shocking number of autistic people who now have long-lasting police records under a secretive programme. “There is no excuse for unleashing this much suspicion against autistic people,” he said. The security minister, Dan Jarvis, said the record number of referrals underlined the scale of the challenge faced in protecting the public from terrorism. “The statistics also show the crucial role the programme plays in keeping the public safe, with more than 6,000 people moved away from violent ideologies that could have resulted in harm to themselves or others. “We will continue to improve Prevent to ensure it has the tools it needs to do its job of stopping people from becoming terrorists or supporting terrorism. We all have a role to play in keeping each other safe and spotting the signs of radicalisation.” Explore more on these topics Prevent strategy Counter-terrorism policy Far right UK security and counter-terrorism England Wales news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://thecatholicherald.com/article/po.text: Search The Catholic Herald August 26, 2026 August 25, 2026 12:00 PM Polish bishops warn reforms are marginalising religion in schools The Catholic Herald The Catholic Herald More Education Europe Related Michael Haynes Lichtenstein parliament votes to legalise abortion The Catholic Herald Government raises estimate of assisted suicide deaths by 60 per cent Christine Rousselle Former St Agnes church demolished following fire Min read share The Polish bishops’ conference has criticised a number of educational reforms which it says are “worrying” and marginalise religion in schools. Starting from September, the Ministry of Education has halved religious education hours per week from two to one and introduced compulsory health education. In an August 24 statement entitled “Young People Deserve More”, the Polish bishops also noted their concern that religious lessons were to be placed before or after compulsory classes, the possibility of combining classes and changes to grading which it said marginalised the subject in schools. The bishops appealed for the “immediate restoration of the proper place for these activities”, as well as a dialogue between the ministry and representatives of religious communities. The bishops stated that the religious education classes, which focus heavily on Church teaching, “are not a privilege of the Church” but rather a “constitutional right of pupils and parents, resulting from the principle of freedom of conscience and religion and the right of parents to raise their children in accordance with their own beliefs”. “Religion lessons help to form conscience, teach responsibility and build a hierarchy of values. They do not serve only the personal formation of believers. They allow you to learn more about the history of Poland and Europe, literature, art, social ethics and many other areas of culture. “They also help to better understand oneself, to find the meaning of life, to deepen the understanding of one's faith. They bring something unique to school education: an answer to the deepest questions about the meaning, value and purpose of human life. For many students, especially in moments of crisis, it is the content learned from religion lessons that turns out to be a signpost that does not allow you to get lost.” Regarding compulsory health education, the statement noted that its concern lay with the “vision of man, marriage and family, which emerges from the curriculum assumptions and published textbooks”, stating that it accepted “with concern” the decision by the Ministry of Education, which will come into effect from September 1. “The upbringing of such a sensitive sphere of human life must respect the right of parents to decide on its shape. The state should support the family in its upbringing, and not take over its basic functions. Sexuality should be presented in the perspective of marital and family relationships, because in this context it serves the authentic good of the human person,” it read. The bishops stated that the lack of an unambiguous position that marriage constituted the union between a man and a woman was “worrying” and asked parents to remain vigilant regarding the education of their children. The bishops also claimed that there was no broad dialogue during the creation of the curriculum and that the requests of the Church were not taken into account. “We believe that such an important area of education requires a broad social consensus, curricular transparency and real participation of parents and educational environments,” the bishops said. “We appeal for substantive consultations with parents, educational circles and religious communities, as well as the joint development of programme content that respects the worldview of all parents, children and young people.” In May 2025, following the announcement of the changes to the curriculum, the bishops released a statement criticising what it called “propaganda” conducted by media outlets, stating that the changes would result in a “complete change in the perception of family and love”. It implored parents not to agree to the “systemic depravity” of their children “to be carried out under the pretext of the so-called health education”. “For the sake of upbringing and salvation, we appeal to you not to consent to the participation of your children in these demoralising activities,” the statement read. https://www.politico.eu/article/european.text: The European Parliament is to open an office in Canada, Parliament President Roberta Metsola announced Monday. The announcement comes two days before Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is due to attend the State of the Union speech at Parliament’s Strasbourg headquarters on Wednesday. Carney will also address the Parliament on Thursday. The Canadian leader is heading to Europe to deepen ties with partners as Ottawa remains locked in a trade war with Washington. Advertisement Advertisement “A stronger presence that facilitates parliamentary exchanges across the Atlantic, with a regional remit reaching as far as the Arctic,” Metsola wrote on social media after a meeting of the Parliament leadership at which they backed the initiative. “Europe and Canada: old friends, still writing the next page together.” The move will see Parliament representatives working in an “antenna office” alongside the existing EU delegation to Canada in Ottawa, which is managed by the European External Action Service. The Parliament office “will also provide an important platform for parliamentary engagement on issues of growing strategic importance to both the EU and Canada,” said a press release from the Parliament. The Parliament has had an office in Ukraine since September 2025. It also has a presence in non-EU countries, including Ethiopia (for relations with the African Union), Moldova, the U.K., Indonesia, the U.S. and Panama.
